d: How an LP divides its portfolio across asset classes, including a target share for private markets. It sets how much the LP commits to funds each year.
x: A pension targeting 15% private equity and 10% private credit.
A family office allocating 30% to alternatives.
s: Private equity reaches 20% against a 15% target.
The LP slows new commitments or sells interests.
The LP increases annual commitments and hires staff.

d: An LP's plan for how much to commit each year to reach and hold its target allocation, given that commitments are drawn over years and returned later.
x: €100m a year spread across five managers.
Pacing model run quarterly.
s: NAV stays high; pacing is cut.
Allocation target takes years to reach.

d: Committing more than the cash an LP currently holds for private markets, expecting that not all commitments will be drawn at once and that distributions will fund later calls.
x: Commitments at 140% of target allocation.
Overcommitment ratio of 1.3x.
s: The LP may face a liquidity squeeze.

d: When listed assets fall faster than private marks, the private share of the portfolio rises above target even though nothing was bought, forcing LPs to slow commitments or sell.
x: Equities fall 25%; private equity share jumps from 15% to 19%.
LPs pausing re-ups in 2022.
s: LP is over-allocated after a market fall.
It sells interests on the secondary market or skips re-ups.

d: An existing LP committing to a manager's next fund. Re-up rates are a strong signal to new LPs.
x: 80% of Fund I LPs re-upped in Fund II.
An LP re-upping at a larger size.

d: The LP's process for choosing funds: sourcing, investment diligence, operational diligence, references and terms review. Most valuable in strategies with wide return dispersion.
x: A pension reviewing 200 funds a year to back 10.
An LP scoring managers on team, strategy, track record and alignment.
s: LP picks based on brand alone.

d: LP review of a manager's operations: valuation, cash controls, compliance, IT and cybersecurity, service providers and governance. Separate from investment diligence and often has veto power.
x: An ODD team visiting the manager's office.
A cybersecurity questionnaire.
s: One person can move cash alone.
ODD flags a control gap; LP may require dual signatures.

d: An adviser that recommends funds to institutional LPs, runs diligence and sometimes has discretion to commit. Getting a consultant's buy rating opens many LP doors.
x: A consultant advising 50 pension funds.
A discretionary gatekeeper committing for clients.
s: Many LPs will not commit without its rating.

d: LP programmes that set aside capital for first- to third-time funds, sometimes through a fund of funds, accepting more risk for access and upside.
x: A state pension emerging manager programme.
A FoF specialising in Fund Is.
s: Successful managers move into the main programme.

d: A model forecasting a fund's calls, distributions and NAV over time. The Takahashi-Alexander (Yale) model is a common starting point.
x: Projecting calls of 25% a year for four years.
Stress testing distributions at half the base rate.
s: Model shows when cash is needed.
LP updates assumptions and liquidity buffers.

d: Committing steadily across years so the portfolio is not concentrated in one market cycle.
x: Equal commitments every year for ten years.
An LP avoiding a big 2021 bet.
s: Steady pacing avoids overweighting high-priced vintages.

d: Managing cash so an LP can always meet capital calls, using cash buffers, credit lines, distributions and secondary options.
x: Holding 10% of unfunded commitments in cash.
Credit line for call coverage.

d: Recording the fund's transactions, valuations, fees and allocations to produce financial statements and LP capital accounts, under IFRS, Lux GAAP, US GAAP or Ind AS.
x: Quarterly closes by the administrator.
Investment entity accounting under IFRS 10.

d: How the fund's income, gains and losses are allocated among partners' capital accounts, matching the waterfall and tax rules.
x: Targeted capital account allocations.
Allocation following distribution provisions.
s: Allocations exclude it from that deal.

d: Secure online access for LPs to notices, reports, capital accounts and tax documents.
x: Quarterly reports posted to a portal.
Capital call notices with payment details.
s: Portals and call-back checks reduce payment fraud.

d: Investors buying minority stakes in fund management firms, receiving a share of fees and carry. Provides capital for GP commitments, succession and growth.
x: A specialist fund buying 15% of a mid-market GP.
Proceeds used to fund the GP commitment.
s: GPs explain use of proceeds and governance.

d: Transferring leadership, economics and decision power from founders to the next generation. LPs assess it before re-upping.
x: Founders reducing carry share over two funds.
Next-generation partners joining the IC.

d: The manager's policies, monitoring and testing to meet regulatory obligations: marketing, conflicts, personal dealing, AML, data protection, reporting.
x: Annual compliance review.
Compliance monitoring plan.

d: Protecting the manager's systems and data, including investor information and payment processes. LP ODD increasingly tests it.
x: Multi-factor authentication for all staff.
Phishing simulations.
s: Business email compromise diverts a distribution.
Call-back verification would have prevented it.
Notification duties under data protection laws.

d: Insurance covering claims against the GP, manager, directors and officers, including portfolio board directors. Who pays the premium is an LPA issue.
x: €20m GPL policy.
Policy covering partners on portfolio boards.

d: The process of moving an LP's interest to a new owner: GP consent, transfer agreement, KYC on the buyer and update of the register.
x: Secondary buyer replacing a pension.
Transfer to an affiliate.
s: Allocation of income split by date.

d: Managing currency risk when fund currency differs from investment or investor currency, at fund, feeder or LP level.
x: Euro fund investing in Indian rupee assets.
Yen-hedged feeder.
s: Interest rate gaps make hedging expensive.

d: EU directive regulating managers of alternative investment funds: authorisation, capital, depositary, leverage, reporting and marketing. AIFMD II (Directive 2024/927) applied from 16 April 2026, adding a loan-origination regime, mandatory liquidity tools for open-ended funds and tighter delegation and fee disclosure.
x: A Luxembourg AIFM authorised by the CSSF.
AIFMD II loan origination rules for a private credit fund.
s: Registers rather than full authorisation, without passport.
Must select at least two liquidity tools.

d: Tools that control redemptions in open-ended funds: gates, notice periods, redemption fees, swing pricing, suspension. Under AIFMD II each open-ended AIF must select at least two.
x: 5% quarterly gate plus 90-day notice.
Anti-dilution levy.
s: AIFMD II gives regulators intervention powers.

d: AIFMD II rules for funds that lend: risk retention, concentration limits, leverage caps and a preference for loan-originating funds to be closed-ended. Funds established before 15 April 2024 have grandfathering in some respects.
x: A private credit fund keeping 5% of loans it sells.
Concentration limit on a single borrower.
s: Must show liquidity is compatible or be closed-ended.

d: ESMA guidelines restricting use of ESG, sustainability, transition and impact terms in EU fund names unless thresholds and exclusions are met. Applied to new funds from May 2025 and existing funds from November 2025.
x: A fund renamed to drop 'sustainable'.
Minimum 80% of investments meeting characteristics.
s: Aligned funds expected to stay compliant.

d: India's framework for privately pooled funds, the SEBI (AIF) Regulations 2012, amended many times since, with an updated Master Circular in 2026. Sets categories, corpus, minimum investment, continuing interest, investment limits, reporting and winding up.
x: Quarterly reports to SEBI.
Annual PPM compliance audit.
s: Liquidation period of one year applies.

d: Under SEBI's April 2026 amendments and June 2026 circular, an AIF scheme may retain liquidation proceeds beyond its fund life in defined situations (pending litigation, regulatory demands, residual expenses) and apply for Inoperative Fund status with reduced compliance.
x: A scheme holding back proceeds for a tax dispute.
A legacy VCF applying for Inoperative Fund status.
s: Tax claim pending at end of fund life.
Scheme retains funds under the circular's conditions instead of distributing all proceeds.
Fund has no assets but a lawsuit.

d: International Financial Services Centres Authority, the single regulator for GIFT City, including its fund management regime under the Fund Management Regulations 2025.
x: FME registration with IFSCA.
PPM taken on record by IFSCA.

d: France's financial markets regulator. It authorises portfolio management companies, approves retail funds and receives declarations for professional funds such as FPCI and SLP.
x: FPCI declared to the AMF.
AMF authorisation of a new AIFM.
s: Notification and annual fee per fund.

d: Luxembourg's financial regulator. It authorises AIFMs and supervises SIFs, SICARs and Part II funds; RAIFs are supervised indirectly through their AIFM.
x: CSSF authorisation of a ManCo.
LMT selection filed via CSSF module.
s: No CSSF product approval; AIFM is supervised.

a: Commission de Contrôle des Activités Financières
d: Monaco's financial regulator. It licenses investment service providers and fund managers, oversees Monaco funds and sets marketing rules. Unlicensed firms may not market to Monaco private residents.
x: CCAF licence for a Monaco SAM managing portfolios.
CCAF oversight of a Monaco FCP.
s: An EU AIFM wants Monaco clients.
Needs a CCAF-authorised distributor or its own CCAF licence.
A Monaco firm distributes a foreign fund.
It acts under its own liability and CCAF rules.

d: Monaco's anti-money-laundering law (Law 1.362 of 2009, amended) supervised by the AMSF. Monaco was grey-listed by FATF in June 2024 and removed in October 2026; it was added to the EU high-risk list in August 2025.
x: Enhanced KYC on a Monaco-based LP by an EU administrator.
Monaco firm's AML risk assessment.
s: EU fund onboards a Monaco family office in 2025.
Enhanced due diligence applied due to EU high-risk listing.
Check whether the EU list has been updated before relaxing checks.

d: UK regulator for AIFMs. In July 2026 it consulted (CP26/28) on a new regime with small, medium and large tiers based on NAV (£750m and £5bn thresholds), removing most small registered managers, with implementation envisaged for 2028.
x: A London AIFM authorised by the FCA.
A small registered real estate manager facing authorisation.
s: Small AIFM tier with lighter rules.
Plan for authorisation under the new regime.

d: Managers advising US private funds register with the SEC under the Investment Advisers Act or rely on exemptions for venture capital advisers and smaller private fund advisers. Funds usually avoid registration under 3(c)(1) or 3(c)(7) and raise under Regulation D.
x: An exempt reporting adviser filing parts of Form ADV.
A registered adviser with $2bn AUM.
s: May lose VC exemption if non-qualifying assets exceed limits.

d: US rule governing advertisements by registered advisers, including how performance is shown: net alongside gross, standard periods, no cherry-picking, substantiation of claims.
x: Showing net IRR with gross IRR in a pitch deck.
Hypothetical performance restricted to suitable audiences.
s: Cherry-picking breaches the rule unless the full set is available.

d: The registration and disclosure form for US investment advisers, updated annually within 90 days of fiscal year end and when material changes occur.
x: Annual amendment by 31 March.
Exempt reporting advisers completing Part 1.

d: Confidential US regulatory report on private funds filed by SEC-registered advisers. 2024 amendments' compliance date has been pushed to 1 July 2027; an April 2026 proposal would raise the filing threshold to $1bn.
x: Annual Form PF for PE advisers by 30 April.
Quarterly event reports within 60 days.
s: Files today; may be exempt if proposal is adopted.
Section 6 report due within 60 days of quarter end.

d: Periodic regulatory reports under AIFMD on each AIF's exposures, leverage, liquidity and investors, with frequency depending on AUM. AIFMD II changes to reporting apply from 2027.
x: Annual Annex IV for a small AIF.
Quarterly reporting for large leveraged AIFs.

d: Identity checks on investors and their beneficial owners, sanctions screening and anti-money-laundering controls, done before a commitment is accepted and refreshed on a risk basis.
x: Verifying the ultimate beneficial owner of a trust LP.
Enhanced checks on a politically exposed person.
s: LP refuses to disclose beneficial owners.

d: The Financial Action Task Force sets global AML/CFT standards and lists jurisdictions under increased monitoring (grey list) or high risk (black list). Listing increases due diligence costs for those jurisdictions.
x: Monaco grey-listed June 2024, removed October 2026.
FATF Recommendation 10 on customer due diligence.
s: LP based in a grey-listed country.

d: Public or restricted registers of the individuals who ultimately own or control companies and funds, such as Luxembourg's RBE.
x: Filing the fund's UBOs in the RBE.
Indian significant beneficial owner rules.
s: Senior managing officials may be listed.

d: Ensuring no investor, portfolio company or counterparty is a sanctioned person, under EU, UN, US (OFAC), UK and other regimes.
x: Screening LPs daily against lists.
Divesting a company after new sanctions.
s: LP's owner added to a list.

d: Rules on handling personal data of investors, staff and portfolio contacts. GDPR applies in the EU; India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and Monaco's own law apply locally.
x: Privacy notice in the subscription booklet.
Data processing agreement with the administrator.
s: Retention duties under AML may override.

d: Indian foreign exchange rules: if an AIF's sponsor or manager is owned or controlled by non-residents, its investments are treated as indirect foreign investment and must follow foreign investment conditions.
x: Foreign-owned manager making an AIF's investments indirect FDI.
Sectoral caps applying to downstream deals.
s: AIF invests in a sector with FDI caps.

d: Controls preventing misuse of material non-public information about listed companies, including portfolio companies after IPO and public targets.
x: Restricted list for listed holdings.
Wall-crossing procedures.

d: AIFMD requires remuneration policies for AIFMs, including carry, with disclosure in annual reports and proportionality for smaller managers.
x: Annual report disclosing total remuneration.
Deferral rules applied proportionately.

d: Conditions for an AIFM to delegate portfolio or risk management, avoiding letterbox entities. AIFMD II adds reporting on delegation arrangements.
x: Luxembourg AIFM delegating advice to an Indian manager.
Delegation notified to the regulator.
s: AIFM must monitor and can terminate.

d: Requirements to keep fund and AML records for a minimum period, often five years after the relationship or fund ends (AIFMD, SEC Rule 204-2, SEBI Regulation 28).
x: Archiving IC minutes and valuation evidence.
Retaining KYC files five years after an LP exits.
s: Regulator requests records after fund closure.

d: The risk that a fund or manager is taxed in a country because decisions are taken or people work there. Managed with board composition, decision location and substance.
x: Luxembourg board meetings held in Luxembourg.
Indian safe harbour for offshore fund managers (section 9A).
s: Partners sign deals from home in another country.
Tax authority may claim a taxable presence.
Section 9A conditions avoid PE if met.

d: Tax reporting regimes under which funds identify investors' tax residence and report account information to tax authorities.
x: Collecting W-8BEN-E forms.
Annual CRS report to Luxembourg tax authority.

d: The fund itself is not taxed; income and gains flow through and are taxed in investors' hands. Indian Cat I and II AIFs have pass-through status for income other than business income.
x: SCSp transparent for Luxembourg tax.
Cat II AIF passing capital gains to investors.
s: Cat II AIF earns business income.

d: How carry is taxed for team members, as capital gain, income or a special regime, varies by country and often depends on holding periods and co-investment.
x: UK carried interest regime.
French carry taxed as capital gains if conditions are met.

d: Tax deducted at source on dividends, interest or gains paid across borders. The right holding structure can reduce it through treaty access, subject to anti-abuse rules.
x: Dividend withholding reduced by treaty.
Interest withholding on shareholder loans.

d: Situations where the manager's interests may differ from LPs', such as cross-fund deals, fees from portfolio companies or GP-led secondaries. Usually need disclosure and LPAC consent.
x: Fund II buying from Fund I.
Manager affiliate providing paid services to companies.

d: Quarterly reports with portfolio updates, valuations, fees and capital account statements, plus audited annual accounts. ILPA templates set a common format.
x: Quarterly report within 45–60 days.
Annual audited accounts within 120 days.

d: Triggered when key persons stop meeting their time commitment. The investment period is suspended until LPs approve replacements or vote to continue.
x: Suspension lasting until LP vote.
Termination of investment period if no vote within 180 days.

d: LPs may remove the GP for fraud, wilful misconduct, gross negligence or material breach, usually by a simple or two-thirds majority, often with reduced carry for the removed GP.
x: Removal by majority after a court finding of fraud.
Carry forfeited on removal.

d: LPs holding a supermajority, typically 66–80% of commitments, may remove the GP or end the investment period without showing cause.
x: 75% vote to end the investment period.
Removal with carry reduction.
s: LPs use no-fault to stop new investments.
